The Band-tailed fruiteater (Pipreola intermedia) is a strikingly colored cotinga endemic to the humid montane forests of the northern Andes, yet detailed life-history data for the species remain sparse. Recent field studies have begun to illuminate key developmental parameters, particularly regarding the early stages of its life cycle. For instance, the incubation period is relatively protracted, with eggs held at a constant developmental temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C] requiring approximately 20 days [ab = approximately 20 days] to hatch. The neonate emerges at a remarkably modest size, with an initial wet body mass of just 5 grams [Ww0 = 5 grams]. This low mass at hatching is characteristic of altricial nestlings that depend heavily on biparental provisioning during the first weeks of life. The small size of the hatchling imposes significant energetic demands on the parents, as the chick must rapidly accumulate tissue before it can achieve thermal independence and, eventually, fledge from the nest.

As the nestling develops under the warm conditions typical of its Andean cloud forest habitat, it undergoes a rapid phase of mass gain and feather development. Under normothermic conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the time from hatching to the achievement of sustained flight, marking fledging, is approximately 20 days [tx = approximately 20 days]. This relatively brief nestling period is notable for a bird of its size class and may reflect selective pressures to minimize predation risk in a high-mortality environment. During this period, parental investment is intense, with both adults contributing to food delivery. The growth trajectory from the 5-gram hatchling to a much larger juvenile is steep, underscoring the efficiency with which the chick converts ingested fruit and insects into structural tissue. The thermal environment remains a critical constraint on developmental rates throughout this phase.

Sexual maturation in the Band-tailed fruiteater occurs after a prolonged juvenile period, a pattern consistent with the relatively slow life history of many Neotropical frugivores. Under typical thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the onset of gonadal activity, marking the attainment of puberty, is estimated to occur at approximately 60 days after hatching [tp = approximately 60 days after hatching]. This timing suggests that the species delays reproductive investment relative to the completion of structural growth, likely because the acquisition of foraging skills and establishment of a territory are prerequisites for successful breeding. The extended interval between fledging and puberty may also reflect the energetic constraints imposed by a diet that, while rich in lipids from fruits, can be seasonally variable in availability. Such a developmental schedule is typical of species with low adult mortality rates, where delayed reproduction may enhance lifetime fitness.

Reproduction in the Band-tailed fruiteater is characterized by a modest annual output, consistent with its life-history strategy as a long-lived tropical bird. Females typically produce a clutch of 1 to 2 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 1 to 2 eggs per nesting attempt], and field observations suggest that they may initiate approximately 1.5 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 clutches per year], a rate that likely varies with local fruit abundance. The time from the individual's own birth to the initiation of its first successful brood has been quantified at around 511 days [tR = around 511 days], measured under stable thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], representing the age at first reproduction. This delay between achieving puberty and commencing actual breeding effort is ecologically significant, as it may reflect the time required for a young bird to secure a high-quality territory and form a stable pair bond. The combination of small clutch size and deferred first reproduction aligns with the broader pattern seen across other members of the Cotingidae.

Adult females of the species reach a maximum recorded body mass of 52 grams [Wwi = 52 grams], a value that falls within the upper range of reported field weights for the species and represents the ultimate wet weight for breeding individuals. Basal metabolic demands at this body size have been measured through respirometry, revealing a maximum resting oxygen consumption rate of 110.91 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 110.91 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This metabolic rate is consistent with values for other cotingas of similar mass and reflects the energetic costs of maintaining a high body temperature in a cool, montane environment. Longevity data, though limited, indicate that the species can achieve a maximum lifespan of approximately 11.4 years [am = approximately 11.4 years] under field conditions, a relatively extended life span that aligns with its delayed reproduction and low annual fecundity at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This suite of life-history traits—small initial mass, protracted development, low reproductive output, and elevated longevity—positions Pipreola intermedia as a classic slow-living endotherm within its Andean cloud forest community.
